speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (for the Deputy Prime Minister) moved
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-83, an Act to amend the Senate and the House of Commons Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, all Members of the House can be proud of the success of parliamentary reform. That parliamentary reform has taken place not only in terms of the changes to the Standing Orders, but also in terms of the duties which all Members of Parliament perform on behalf of their Party and on behalf of the House.
These additional duties refer to the standing committee chairmen, the panel of chairmen who deal with legislative committees, as well as to the House Leaders' offices, the Deputy House Leader, the Party Whips and the caucus chairmen.
Under those circumstances, the Government has brought forward Bill C-83 after full and complete discussions with the other Party House Leaders. This Bill was introduced in June of this year but was not proceeded with at that time. There has been full discussion with the other Parties and it is my understanding that all three Parties will support this Bill.
It is not our intention to debate it at any length and we would ask that there be unanimous consent that it go to Committee of the Whole and be dealt with expeditiously as soon as second reading is completed. It is also my understanding that no recorded division will be requested.
This Bill is recognition of the work-load that all Members of Parliament take on in addition to their duties as Members. It impacts on the time they have available for those duties and impacts upon the time they have in their ridings. For those reasons, it was the opinion of Members of all three Parties that they should be compensated for undertaking those duties. I commend this Bill to the House and appreciate the support and encouragement of my colleagues.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can confirm what the Government House Leader has said with regard to the extensive consultation about this Bill among all the Parties. I also want to confirm that we are in agreement with the procedure that the Minister has proposed for dealing with the Bill.
It has become apparent that one of the results of parliamentary reform that was put into effect some months ago has been the development of not just a more extensive and active committee system but one that involves a large number of meetings. The committee chairpersons are required not only to preside over the committee meetings but to do a lot of the behind-the-scenes organizational work. The system created as a result of the parliamentary reform, which has been effective, has resulted in many layers, if I may describe it that way, which make demands of the committee chairpersons that were not made before.
It is clear that the development of the system of the House of Commons as a result of these rule changes has placed additional duties on a number of people. There are precedents for what is proposed in this Bill in what already exists in a number of the provincial legislatures.
Due to the intent or spirit of the reports on parliamentary reform, which have been well received in the House, due to the changes in the rules to which the House has agreed, and the additional work-loads that have developed as a result, and due to the precedents which exist in a number of the provincial legislatures, I think that the Bill presented by the Deputy House Leader (Mr. Lewis) should be supported. We are ready to concur with the procedure which he has suggested.

The House resumed from Monday, September 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, allow me to get squared away because I am a little awkward on my feet.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. On a previous occasion in this House when one of my colleagues was in a similar situation the House gave him permission to speak from his seat. If the Member is interested, perhaps we could give him the same opportunity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for the offer. I may indeed take advantage of it before my 20 minutes are up. Having spent eight years in this Chamber I am used to trying to deliver my speech while on my feet, and I would like to at least start that way.
I would like to tell Members of the House, the people in the Gallery, and those watching us on television that I am especially happy to be here today. Except for the benefit of a seat-belt on Sunday I am absolutely certain I would not have this opportunity to speak to this Bill. I commend the use of seat-belts to those who sometimes get a little lazy in that area, as I think we all do from time to time.
My accident occurred between Geneva and Lausanne. I was in Switzerland because I had spent the previous week as a
member of the Canadian delegation to the Executive Committee of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. This organization is made up of countries and delegations from around the world that are concerned about the issue of refugees and what this Parliament is about to do with regard to refugee legislation.
It was particularly exciting to be at that meeting in Geneva because once again, in keeping with the spirit of the UNHCR decision to award us the Nansen Medal a year ago, the Canadian delegation was in the forefront of changing patterns and changing trends. We are viewed in the international community as a leading nation, if not the leading nation, when it comes to humanity, compassion and concern for the refugees of this world.
There has been so much discord within our country. Very eminent Canadians have spoken out against this legislation. Members of the Opposition and, indeed, one or two members of my own Party have spoken with conviction, passion, and concern against the legislation.
I was able to spend hours in Geneva with those who are considered to be world-wide legal experts in the United Nations High Commission for Refugees. I spent time with the Commissioner himself, with the Deputy Commissioner, with delegations from every nation in the world concerned about the Canadian legislation. There is no other conclusion possible than that this is the finest Immigration Act, that these amendments proposed by Bill C-55 will give us the finest system in the world. Nobody else comes close. As one goes to those other people and asks them to show us another nation that will provide in legislative form the rights and privileges for true refugees, they cannot come up with one.
This Chamber during third reading debate and, hopefully, the members in the other place will put this legislation into place quickly. It is indeed the model for the rest of the world to follow.
How did we come to the discord? In part, the original drafting was flawed. It is a complex piece of legislation. It is part of an over-all Immigration Act. There were mistakes made in the original drafting. People have not caught up with the reality that Members of this Chamber called the most expert witnesses in the country, questioned them, listened to them and amended that original drafting. Well over 50 amendments were made. The Bill that we will be voting on shortly, I hope, and sending to the Senate, has to be seen not in its original form but as an amended Bill.
We have to pay tribute in the House to the members who served on that legislative committee with diligence, compassion, caring and skill. We have to pay tribute to the nongovernmental organizations in the community which took the time and the trouble to come to tell us what they saw or did not see in the Bill. The group we often overlook is the task force itself, some of whose members have worked on this
October 16, 1987

problem for four or five years, through two different Governments, trying to arrive at changes that would work. They have worked long, hard and with great skill.
But in the process of consultation discord was created. Many members of the NGO community have a great deal of difficulty trusting the bureaucracy, the civil servants in the Immigration Department. With the passage of time many people in the Immigration Department have a great deal of difficulty trusting those leaders in the NGO community. The relationship has degenerated into a slanging-match. A lot of unkind things are said privately, and sometimes publicly.
I would like to say that I fail to see how any of that advances our humanitarian and compassionate consideration for the refugees of the world. It is a luxury that we enjoy a democracy in Canada where we do have freedom of speech. But what purpose is served by using ugly words, by calling others down and by spreading false rumours?
It has been a difficult process to arrive at Bill C-55. But that process is now behind us. It is time, I think, and it is time, I hope, for all those people who care about refugees in the world to come back together and begin to work together. The cause is just.
If one looks at the world today one will see that not every country enjoys a democracy. Very few countries, perhaps as many as 35 or 36, have systems of Government that we would recognize as democracies. That is out of 160 countries. Even democracies can be guilty of persecution. But in those countries that are not democracies it is almost a guarantee that persecution does occur, based on political beliefs in many cases, based on race, based on religion, based on social groups.
I think we have a particular obligation as one of the world's finest democracies, today, tomorrow, and forever to have an open-door policy, to welcome the victims of persecution. If we want the world some day to enjoy our kind of democracy and our system, then we have to offer sanctuary to those who fight for it in repressive regimes, those who are victims of that kind of behaviour in repressive regimes. If we offer sanctuary, and if other western and other democratic nations offer sanctuary, then the struggle will continue and the world will change. It will be a better place. But the failure to offer sanctuary could spell the death-knell of progress of that kind.
What about our legislation? Why do I say it is a model? Why do others say it is so terrible? I think the biggest difference between us is probably the degree of understanding we might have about the entire system. It is a complex system and it is difficult to understand. Most of the criticism comes about because people look at a piece of the system. They do not have the knowledge to see that piece in the context of the whole.
In 1978 the Immigration Act came into effect. Lying at the core of our current Immigration Act is the responsibility, the power, for the Minister of Immigration to act in a humanitarian and compassionate manner in any individual case.
Immigration Act, 1976
Much of what we have done in the last decade for refugees, and in the decade before that, has been based on that principle in the Immigration Act. Nothing we are about to do in Bill C-55 changes that. That power is there today. That obligation is there today. That power and that obligation will be there tomorrow. It will be exercised.
We heard testimony that today the Minister exercises that power at the end of a chain. When somebody faces deportation from Canada it is exercised. In the new world it will be there from the first day of arrival until the day somebody leaves. There will be instructions to utilize it up front. So when someone who is clearly a refugee arrives undocumented at our border point, having fled persecution, what I think people fail to understand is that it is the intention of the Government, the bureaucracy, and it is the power within the Act, that in that initial interview with the immigration officer a ministerial permit simply has to be issued and the person is inside Canada.
There is a bogyman out there that we will put every single arrival at the border through inquiry. That is ridiculous. It would be an enormous waste of resources. It would serve no purpose to proceed in that fashion. Humanitarian and compassionate considerations will be the first thing taken into account. People will be given permits and landed in Canada when it is clear that they have a legitimate claim to our protection.
An inquiry is based on a decision by an immigration officer at the border point, agreed to by that person's supervisor, that there is no good reason to admit this person to Canada. Two people have to reach the decision not to admit, and then our legislation takes over.
The legislation before us today states that we immediately assign a barrister and solicitor to the applicant paid for at taxpayers' expense. An inquiry will be held in front of an adjudicator, who is like a judge, and a member of the refugee board. There are two decision-makers. The claimant has a lawyer. No country in the world does that. This is still at the point of admission.
In most European nations an officer at the border says, "No", and there is no protection, there is no appeal, there is nothing.
In our system two officers have to concur. When the claimant does not agree, a lawyer is provided, and two people are provided to make the decision. If they agree with the two bureaucrats that the person does not need protection according to the clauses in the Bill, then entry cannot be denied for an additional 24 hours. This piece of legislation provides a lawyer to prepare an appeal to the Federal Court of Canada, a leave application, and a period of 24 hours for an additional appeal to the Minister.
Six people representing five organizations all must agree that this person should not be admitted to Canada. We are

October 16, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
talking about quality of protection for legitimate refugees. Is it conceivable that six people representing five different organizations who ail agree that this person has no basis to the claim to need protection would be wrong? They do not have to decide that the claim is legitimate and that the person is a refugee. They simply have to decide that there is absolutely no evidence to suggest that the person could be found to be a refugee. That is the manner in which the decision not to admit must be upheld.
I hear somebody state that is very fair. It is more than very fair. It may be too much protection. But it is clearly the most protection in the world, by a country mile. No country provides that protection to a claimant for potential entry into a country.
Once inside the country, as people move through the determination process, there has been a lot of concern about what people call the lack of an appeal. What is overlooked in the discussion is that we have an informal hearing with two members of a refugee board, both of whom have to say that the person is not a refugee before the status is denied. This is an informal hearing which can go on for hours. It is done in a relaxed atmosphere. Claimants may bring anyone to testify on their behalf. They can introduce any evidence. The Crown must provide evidence on past decision-making related to people of this characteristic. The statute requires that that must be part of the evidentiary base.
Let us assume that they conclude that the person is not a refugee. There is no immediate removal. There is a leave application to the Federal Court to have the case reconsidered. The estimates are that it will take at least two months for the court to decide. In the interim, we have the Act itself. There is a humanitarian and compassionate obligation on the Minister, and two months for the NGO, for the church, for a brother or a sister, for a Member of Parliament, for a barrister and solicitor familiar with the case to go directly to the Minister on appeal of this decision. That exists in the scheme of the Act and it is not being taken away. Therefore, there are two types of appeals which flow from a negative decision in terms of the statute that we are providing to the Elouse and to the nation.
Nowhere else in the world today are there those types of conditions; the provision of a barrister or solicitor, the different levels, the humanitarian and compassionate grounds. I ask myself, why do we have such anger and turmoil? Why are such statements made? The answer is that we have lived through a period of history, and we have gone through close to 10 years of the current Immigration Act. The scheme of the Act as it sits without these amendments requires employees of the Immigration Department domestically to keep their hands off refugees. They never sit in on the hearings.
The Department is currently charged with the administration of the Act and whether the person has a legal right to enter Canada. If they decide that he or she does not, they send the matter to inquiry. In inquiry the person makes a claim to be a refugee, and it must be adjourned. Therefore, all the
employees of the Department are screened out. The only other relationship that the Department has is one person does an examination under oath. Two, three, or four months later that transcript then goes to RSAC, it is appealed to the Immigration Appeal Board and to the Federal Court of Canada. But the immigration employee, the line officer, today has no compassionate power at the border, and no direction to act on behalf of refugees. They do not sit through the inquiry and hear the refugees' stories on credibility and so on.
Where is the refugee right now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Where is the refugee right now? We have some hollering from across the way as to where the refugee is. Some are inside the country on ministerial permits, some are in detention at border points.
I would say to the parliamentary committee, to the NGO community, and to the Minister that now is the time for the dialogue to be commenced. There is a watch-dog rule on the administrative implementation of this Act. The barristers and solicitors, and the NGO communities have a big role to play. The parliamentary committee through its investigative powers can ensure that the entire scheme of the Act is administered with sensitivity.
We as parliamentarians can urge the Minister to provide that type of direction to the bureaucracy, and we can pass legislation. This legislation is a model for the world to follow. We may reach a day in five or ten years time when we may find some manner to improve it. But it is far ahead of any piece of legislation that presently exists in the world in terms of its capacity to provide real protection to real refugees. I urge this Chamber to move it forward this day. I urge members in the other place to look at it, but do so quickly. Let us pass this legislation and regain our rightful place in the world as the leader in terms of legal protection for legitimate refugees.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) stated that the committee heard a wide variety of witnesses, and that it made amendments following their representations. The point that has been emphasized by our Party, and by the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), is that the Government absolutely refused to deal with the fundamental concerns brought forward by the majority of those witnesses.
I would like to read to the Hon. Member the letter which was sent to concerned Members of Parliament from Donald Anderson, General Secretary of the Canadian Council of Churches, dated September 21. I ask him to comment on the substance of the letter concerning Bill C-55. It reads:
We appreciate government work to try to improve Bill C-55. Unfortunately our deep concerns remain. How can we know if a person claiming to be a refugee needs our help if we do not hear their problems? Each person claiming to be a refugee should have a right to have their individual circumstances
October 16, 1987

assessed and their case decided on its merits before competent independent decision makers. To us, this is the intent of the Convention and Protocol.
Immigration programs may legitimately choose who comes on humanitarian grounds and may set priorities on countries they may come from. We understand the attractiveness of this approach. Bill C-55 provides for exclusion of people not on the basis of their individual circumstances, but by a political cabinet decision that the country they transitted before arriving in Canada is deemed to adhere to Clause 33 of the Convention, that is, it is deemed the transit country will not return the person in any manner whatsoever to a country where he or she may face persecution. This is a far shot from our obligation to give an individual who arrives in Canada a fair hearing of his or her claim to need our protection.
Also, there is no meaningful appeal to any of the critical decisions made which can remove claimants from Canada in proposed inquiries or hearings.
We cannot accept legislation which sets aside a claimant's right to just procedures in the name of administrative convenience. We urge you to reconsider, to abandon this Bill C-55 and to speedily replace it with one conforming with the principles of allowing every claimant a hearing on the merits and a meaningful appeal. There are alternative processes we can surely all support.
I urge the Hon. Member to consider the import of the letter and the evidence of other witnesses who appeared before the committee. How can he possibly say that the committee and the Government responded to their very legitimate concerns?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for reading that letter, and 1 thank him particularly for referring to the date of it, because it clearly identifies the problem about which I spoke. The Bill was not through the House on September 21. What the Hon. Member has is a letter dealing with the original drafting, not with Bill C-55 as amended. It could not be, simply because of the date. That is the first problem.
Expressed in the letter is the concern about returning people to what has become known in the popular press as a safe third country. That whole section was amended dramatically and drastically in its wording both in the House and in committee.
First, under statute law the Cabinet of Canada is prohibited from naming a safe country unless it complies clearly with Article 33 of the Convention, which is non-refoulement.
The second major feature of the set of clauses is that the return can only be to the country from where they came, nowhere else in the world.
Let us say that people came here from France and France will not take them back. France has been where they were protected; they were not in the country of persecution. If France will not take them back, they proceed in our system. That is what the clause is all about.
One could not go to the world body and sit with those delegations without coming back to Canada with a very deep concern about the refugee claimant in the orbit phenomenon.
Refugees do not abuse the system of any nation, but bogus claimants do. Bogus claimants have a lot of resources in many cases. They take advantage of legal loopholes and they begin to swamp the generosity of people who care about refugees. It was particularly disturbing to see in the Chamber so many
Immigration Act, 1976
amendments being moved by the Opposition which provided advantages for bogus claimants, not for legitimate refugees.
Our obligation as a nation is to legitimate refugees. Our obligation, in world terms, is to kick bogus claimants out of Canada and to encourage France and Sweden to do likewise.
There is a generosity of spirit which is alive and well, but they cannot continue to abuse it, or it will disappear. The willingness of generous nations to help refugees will go down the tubes world-wide if we do not have a system to differentiate between a real refugee and a bogus claimant. We cannot provide an endless series of loopholes for bogus claimants and expect that they will not use them. The people who will not use them are legitimate refugees, because they do not have the resources.
That indeed may be a potential misunderstanding between Mr. Anderson and myself, to some extent. I know that when our enforcement people in immigration catch people who are in the country illegally and bring them to an inquiry, at the rate of about 1,000 per month, suddenly 75 per cent of them claim to be refugees. It is a magical transformation to avoid enforcement of our law. Bill C-55 corrects that. Bill C-55 is necessary to perfect our collective will to do what needs to be done for legitimate refugees.

Mr. Speaker, I would point out that it still depends upon the Minister's discretion and it is still at the discretion of the Minister's staff. Furthermore, the Hon. Member did not address the second question which I raised, that is, the whole question of some kind of appeal process.
The appeal process is still based upon questions of law rather than upon questions of fact, so that questions of merit are not able to come forward. I would like to hear the Hon. Member's comment on this vital concern of witnesses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to give even more clarity. People arriving at one of our border points who have fled persecution have no documents, no papers, nothing. They can tell their entire story to the immigration officer they first encounter. Any action taken in relationship to that arrival must be approved by a supervisor. If it is a positive feeling that they are really refugees, they simply issue a ministerial permit and the persons are inside the country. The only people they take to inquiry, common sense tells us, are those to whom they wish to deny entry. That is what the legislation says. It is time the nation looked at what the legislation says, not at what other people say it says. That is the scheme of the Act and the amendments in Bill C-55.
If we have 3,800 people arriving from Portugal, claiming to be refugees, and telling their story to the immigration officer, it is difficult to believe the story because there is no available evidence that there is persecution in Portugal. When these people arrive at our borders, under the current situation they are here for two years or three years because of all these wasted appeals.

October 16, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Under the new system these people will go to inquiry and within seven days-perhaps it will be as few as 72 hours-they will have told their story and, if there is nothing to their story, they are gone. They have had appeals. They can appeal to the Minister and move for leave to appeal to the Federal Court.
The inquiry itself is an appeal of an administrative decision made by an officer at the border point. The legislation deals with nothing except appeals and levels of appeals. Six different groups have to concur in the decision not to admit before that person is not admitted. The person has a lawyer throughout, paid for at our expense. No country in the world comes close to the degree of protection offered by Bill C-55.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak to Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act of Canada. The Bill is an extremely important piece of legislation. It reflects, or is supposed to reflect, the heart, the soul and mind of a country made up of so many people who came to these shores either under refugee or immigration status. It sets the future policy of our nation.
I listened to my hon. colleague across the way. I know he is a sincere and well meaning individual and I hope his health improves very quickly. As I see him hobbling out on his crutches, I appreciate the effort he has put forward.
I still remain unconvinced that there is a sense of humanity and sense of consideration for the true, real refugee coming to our shores. That is why I feel so strongly and say to the Minister that if this Bill goes through I hope he will watch it with great care. I hope he will bring the proper kinds of amendments to the Bill so that the three major areas of serious concern; the prescreening; the safe third country and the appeal process, will enable us to be sure that real refugees not bogus refugees will receive proper consideration.
The Member was pleading and discussing the Portugese situation, which only indicates in the strongest way the need for us to reform the immigration guidelines and the need for us to expand the definitions and the kinds of classes that we are prepared to accept in terms of general immigration, namely, the family class and the family rejoinder class.
I do not know what has happened to us in this country. I come from the Province of Quebec where large families were a way of life and only enriched the fabric of society. We have dramatically changed that concept of family in Quebec as we have done elsewhere in North America. That has not been the case in many of the European countries, the eastern countries, the South American and other countries from which immigrants come, and as a result of whom this country is much enriched. In other countries the concept of family is a much larger one. It includes nieces, nephews, aunts, uncles and grandparents.
The sooner we separate out the concerns surrounding refugee Bills, refugees coming to this country and the immigration stream, making it very clear that we are talking about two separate procedures and two separate groups in Canada the better it will be. It may seem as clear as motherhood and apple pie to Members of this House, but it certainly is not clear to the ordinary Canadian citizen.
What about fatherhood and apple pie?
Fatherhood and apple pie. If the Member becomes a good baker, then that is fine with me. We could trade recipes, but that is not the point.
Oh, oh!

The issue is how to bring the important concerns that are addressed in this Bill and remove the confusion found in the immigration stream and that stream which is called the refugee stream.
I find it rather ironic that we are dealing with this Bill in 1987, this being the United Nations International Year of the Homeless. What could be more relevant at the time of the world's focus on homelessness than a group of people, tens of thousands, maybe millions and millions, who are homeless not because of choice but because of instability in their home countries? They are looking for a decent home, a place to set down roots and a place to start a new life for themselves and their children.
This Bill does not answer the needs in the way that it should. Nor does it meet our responsibilities on an international scale. It is not only ironic but it is Machiavellian that we have allowed confusion to exist in the minds of Canadians. People who ask for immigrant status for their extended family but are blocked, who then see this large mass of refugees, who seem by the way in which this issue has been handled to be taking the place of nieces or nephews, it raises anger and ire on the part of our new immigrants. Confusion continues. We need a Government that will educate, lead and articulate that difference between a landed immigrant and those who come to our doors as refugees, allowing the kind of openness to those who have reached our shores in that kind of a situation.
I would suggest that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) should take a good look at the statistics with respect to the amount of family rejoinders that have taken place in Canada. Given the turmoil in the international world, we have far from kept our commitment, both in terms of the economic migrant and immigrant and the immigrant coming for family rejoinder. I would like to see the family rejoinder category enlarged and I am sure the Minister would too. I am sure there are ways in which that can be done and I hope it happens sooner rather than later.
From a historical perspective I think it is important to take a look at what Canada has done. In the 1960s and 1970s Canada was essentially selecting refugees from around the world and we were doing a very good job. We were very concerned and
October 16, 1987

manifesting a humanitarian approach as we went to refugee camps and selected immigrants. In recent years, during the 1980s, things changed. People are creative and when there is tremendous pressure around them and there seems no way out, they find alternative ways and means to enter a country. Those alternate routes are not always the most effective and efficient routes, but human beings who are looking for a new way of life and freedom in this world do accept terrible risks. That is something with which we need to concern ourselves.
In the early 1980s, as the Liberal Government saw this increasing growth of refugees, some of them bogus, some of them coming here using disreputable representatives, Rabbi Plaut was called upon to do a study and to undertake a serious examination of the needs of having an updated and new refugee Bill. A backlog of refugee claimant cases was aggravated by inaction. Rabbi Plaut said at the end of 1984 that the Government should have acted in an expeditious way to meet the growing concern. Did the Government do that? No, Mr. Speaker. What we had was no less than four different Ministers of Immigration, the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald), the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean), The Hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Weiner) and the Hon. Member for Roberval (Mr. Bouchard)-do I have 10 minutes or 20 minutes, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, tonight Overlea Secondary School in my riding will be officially renamed Marc Garneau Collegiate Institute in recognition of Canada's first astronaut in space.
The school, which serves both North York and East York students, will specialize in mathematics, science and high
technology, including computer science and space technology. It will be working in co-operation with the nearby Ontario Science Centre, NASA, the National Research Council of Canada, the Science Council of Canada, the National Museum of Science and Spar Aerospace.
The name Marc Garneau Collegiate was chosen not only to highlight the specialized teaching program but also to provide a role model for the students. It should remind us all that this is the twenty-fifth anniversary of Canada in space, that 50 per cent of the engineers at NASA during the first days of the American Gemini program were Canadians, and that Canadians built the communications antenna and the lunar landing legs for the Apollo program.
Canadians have established themselves as world leaders in science. The students from Marc Garneau Collegiate will be our leaders of the future.

Mr. Speaker, this weekend, women across Canada will demonstrate their strong opposition to Canada's unjust and discriminatory abortion law. Statistics Canada figures show that access to legal abortions is declining dramatically and 18 per cent of therapeutic abortion committees which should be approving legal abortions have approved no abortions at all.
The current law only allows abortions which are performed in hospitals with permission from a panel of three doctors who determine if continuing the pregnancy would endanger a woman's life or health. Section 251 of the Criminal Code forces women to endure unnecessary and dangerous delays. The tragic consequences of this intolerable law fall most heavily on young women, immigrant women, rural women, working-class women and women of colour.
One male columnist expressed what many women feel. To compel a woman to bear a child against her will or to force her to abide by what others define as adequate or inadequate reasons for an abortion is a form of naked authoritarian violence. It is ironic that in this developed nation women must engage in constant struggle to obtain a fundamental right while an international conference on family planning has called on Governments throughout the world to liberalize abortion laws.
I call upon the Government to repeal Sections 251 and 252 of the Criminal Code, to decriminalize abortion, and to introduce a preventive holistic health care system including public community health clinics offering a complete range of health care services, including family planning and access to abortion for women and their families.

1RAN-IRAQ CONFLICT-SUPPORT URGED FOR UNITED NATIONS RESOLUTION

Mr. Speaker, a couple of days ago the Iran-Iraq conflict began affecting more of the innocent civilian population in urban areas. An attack on a school in the Iraqi capital of Bagdad resulted in the deaths of 32 and the wounding of 218 innocent civilians, mostly children.

In view of the existing explosive situation highlighted by this incident, and the prevailing concern of possible involvement of non-belligerent third parties, I wish other Members of this House to join me in expressing sympathy to the families of the victims in Bagdad and expressing in strongest terms support for the efforts of our Government to urge the parties to the Iran-Iraq conflict to abide by the terms of the UN Security Council Resolution 598 of July 20, 1987, which will help restore the much desired peace and stability in the region and put an end to the kind of incident that was witnessed in the senseless slaughter of the children of Baghdad.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Scarborough continues to lead all of Metro Toronto in economic growth and job creation. Over 450 new businesses opened last year, and in the past three years 26,000 new jobs have been created. The largest single employment increase occurred in the manufacturing sector which now employs close to one-third of all Scarborough workers.
Those manufacturers and the workers they employ know that, thanks to the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement, their economic future looks very good indeed. Free trade means that Scarborough's businesses will have greater access to the U.S. market and a chance to compete for some $300 billion worth of U.S. federal government contracts.
Free trade also means that consumers in Scarborough will pay lower prices for the goods they buy and have a wider selection to choose from. The President of the Scarborough Chamber of Commerce welcomed the agreement by saying that free trade will give Scarborough an opportunity to compete in a larger market and, over time, that will help them expand and create new jobs.
Business people, workers and consumers in Scarborough welcome the free trade agreement because they know it will help our city to continue to be one of the most prosperous and industrious communities in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians associated with the Canadian forest industry were shocked and experienced a sense of betrayal when they found that the federal Government had decided to adhere to the American request to impose a 15 per cent softwood tax on exports going to the United States. They were doubly surprised when they found this 15 per cent softwood tax was now entrenched in the Canada-U.S. trade deal.
In some provinces such as British Columbia the provincial Governments have increased stumpage rates at the same time. Mr. Ike Barber, spokesperson for Slocan Timber Products Clearwater Mill indicated that the B.C. Government increased charges to that company more than 1,000 per cent.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity today to participate in debate on Bill C-55 which provides for amendments to the
Immigration Act. My colleagues and I have just tabled a number of petitions. As the House knows and perhaps the people watching do not, Hon. Members were not allowed to read the petitions at the time of presenting them, so as part of my speech on Bill C-55, I would like to read into the record one of the petitions just so it is there for public consideration. It is entitled "Petition to the Honourable House of Commons, in Parliament Assembled.
The petition of the undersigned residents of Canada who now avail themselves of their ancient and undoubted right thus to present a grievance common to your Petitioners in the certain assurance that your honourable House will thereby provide a remedy, humbly sheweth
Whereas Bill C-55 threatens Canada's traditional commitment to assisting refugees, and sets out measures designed to keep most refugee claimants out of the country as opposed to assuring that genuine refugee claimants are given protection, and
Whereas Bill C-55 will result in many, perhaps most, refugees who reach our borders being turned away without having their claim heard on the merits of their case, and
Whereas by limiting the right of appeal to points of law, this legislation ignores the reality that most refugee claims are questions of fact and credibility, and
Whereas the concept of "safe third country" has no foundation in law and no definition and therefore subjects the refugee process to undue political and diplomatic pressures, and
Whereas the Standing Committee of Parliament has proposed a new procedure for refugees which, if adopted, would fairly and effectively solve problems of backlogs and unsubstantiated claims, and
Whereas the alternative has widespread support among all parties in Parliament as well as the Canadian Council of Churches, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress and most other groups and individuals knowledgeable on refugee issues.
Therefore we the undersigned, your Petitioners, humbly pray and call upon the Parliament to ensure that Government and Parliament withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of claims of refugee claimants before a Refugee Board independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to such hearings for every applicant in Canada, and the right to appeal on the basis of fact.
That is the petition that has been circulated across Canada and been signed by hundreds if not thousands of Canadians who are very concerned about the impact of this legislation and about the manner in which those seeking to come to this land are treated.
The Bill revises the Immigration Act of 1976 mainly as it deals with people who claim refugee status in Canada, either when they arrive at a port of entry or when they are already here with visas as immigrants, students or visitors. The great majority of claimants are those arriving at a port of entry, usually without a visa. The Government, particularly the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission, has over a half dozen years tried to twist the system against refugee claimants by screening out ones they consider bogus and not letting them be examined by the body authorized to determine whether or not they are refugees.
A refugee, according to the UN Treaty we signed 20 years ago, is a person outside of his country and unable or unwilling
October 16, 1987

to return through a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, political outlook, or membership in a particular social group.
Canada's present law, the 1976 Immigration Act, provides a system for examination of claimants and decision by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee and Immigration Appeal Board. The system is cumbersome and it broke down two or three years ago because the number of claimants increased faster than the staff provided by the Government.
Once it had broken down, and a claimant might wait two, three or five years for a final decision, the so-called consultants and bogus refugees moved in. For a fee of several thousand dollars per head, consultants arranged to bring people in, coached to make a refugee claim which, given our strong human rights law and broken down processing system, could give them several years to earn Canadian wages before being removed from Canada. The worst example was that of Portuguese claiming to be Jehovah's Witnesses who feared persecution by the Roman Catholic Church in Portugal. The Government delayed imposing visa requirement for 14 months after the scam was known, allowing in 3,500 bogus claimants. Later came the Turks, Brazilians and others.
Quite clearly the law needs revision. The Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, as a result of a study directed to it by the then Minister of State for Immigration and the House, tabled in November, 1985, its fifth report with a proposal for a swift and fair system of refugee status determination.
The committee proposed that a refugee claimant be sent directly to a refugee board without a lot of immigration procedures first. The board would decide yes or no, being trained and authorized to do so, and Immigration would take over from there; either admitting the person on refugee grounds or, if there were no other humanitarian grounds, expelling the person.
The Government was required to reply within four months but it has never provided this House with what we consider a comprehensive response to that report. Instead, it responded with Bill C-55, tabled in May of this year.
Briefly, this Bill sends a refugee claimant first to an immigration inquiry to determine whether there is any reason to not remove him or her from this country. The immigration adjudicator, a member of the refugee division at this inquiry, examines only the eligibility and credibility of the claimant. This means they do not judge the merits of his or her claim but only whether or not that person would be safe in another country which they passed through and should be removed to that country, or whether the country that the person indicates they are fleeing from is in fact a country that does not produce refugees. On either of these grounds they may prohibit him or her from going to the refugee division to state the whole claim and have it determined by that body.
Immigration Act, 1976
Although the Bill has a few good points we have opposed it essentially because of the way it will prevent most claimants from having access to an otherwise good refugee determination system, that is the refugee division. We also oppose the harsh restrictions on time provided to find a lawyer, except for the ones provided and paid for by the Minister, and the severe restrictions on the right of appeal to the courts.
The restrictions on access violates the UN Convention which requires that everyone be accorded the right to make a refugee claim, and the UN Charter of Human Rights which says every persecuted person has the right to seek protection of another Government. It also violates the Supreme Court of Canada decision in the Singh case in April, 1985, that on the basis of the Charter everyone physically in Canada who makes a refugee claim has the right to be heard in person by the body that will decide on the merits of his or her claim. The Charter also guarantees the right of access to counsel. The right to appeal is implicit in Canadian law and may be defended on Charter grounds.
The Bill was tabled in May. We had an emergency session this summer, which is still going on and on and on, to deal with a separate but similar immigration Bill. However, because there was such urgency in dealing with C-55 the committee work was rushed through. There were only seven meeting days and some 40 witnesses were crammed into 44 1/2 hours. Clearly what the Government was trying to do was prevent a groundswell of opposition. It knew once the groups involved in immigration, whether it be the ethnic groups themselves who provide support for the people of their former nationality, or the churches, or labour groups or what have you, got an idea of what this Bill would really do they would develop the kind of groundswell that would be necessary to convince the Government to defeat it.
As we have seen, thousands of people have signed petitions asking the Government to change this. I get calls on a regular basis from churches in my riding who want an update and want to know what they can do, who they can write to, how they can put pressure on the Government to change this legislation. I have a copy of one such letter dated September 21 of this year from Donald Anderson, General Secretary of the Canadian Council of Churches. That is a very well respected body which has as its basis for being, aside from religion, the humanitarian aspects of our society. He writes:
We appreciate government work to try to improve Bill C-55. Unfortunately our deep concerns remain. How can we know if a person claiming to be a refugee needs our help if we do not hear their problems? Each person claiming to be a refugee should have a right to have their individual circumstances assessed and their case decided on its merits before competent independent decision makers. To us, this is the intent of the Convention and Protocol.
Immigration programs may legitimately choose who comes on humanitarian grounds and may set priorities on countries they may come from. We understand the attractiveness of this approach.
Bill C-55 provides for exclusion of people not on the basis of their individual circumstances, but by a political cabinet decision that the country they transitted before arriving in Canada is deemed to adhere to Clause 33 of the Convention, that is, it is deemed the transit country will not return the person in any manner whatsoever to a country where he or she may face persecution.

October 16, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
This is a far shot from our obligation to give an individual who arrives in Canada a fair hearing of his or her claim to need our protection.
Also, there is no meaningful appeal to any of the critical decisions made which can remove claimants from Canada in proposed inquiries or hearings.
We cannot accept legislation which sets aside a claimant's right to just procedures in the name of administrative convenience.
We urge you to reconsider, to abandon this Bill C-55 and to speedily replace it with one conforming with the principles of allowing every claimant a hearing on the merits and a meaningful appeal. There are alternative processes we can surely all support.
Let me spend a few moments going into some detail on the elements I have already referred to; first, the denial of the right to be heard which was not corrected during many attempts in committee by my colleague, the Hon. Member or Spadina (Mr. Heap). 1 would just like to compliment him for the work he has done over this long summer and fall. I want to compliment the Member for Spadina for the many hours he has spent in Ottawa and out on the hustings working with the network that developed opposition to this legislation, working with witnesses and his colleagues on the legislative committee in an attempt to convince the Government of the need to make positive changes to the legislation. He has done an excellent job. I not only compliment him, I thank him on behalf of my constituents and all those who are concerned about immigration matters.
The denial of the right to be heard has not been corrected. The main fault in Bill C-55, quite unchanged by scores of amendments attempted in the legislative committee and at report stage, is that it denies Canada's obligation to let a refugee claimant at our border state his or her case. This is called "universal access", and is supported by the Supreme Court and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The UN Convention and Protocol relating to the status of refugees, which Canada signed in 1967, states unequivocally in Article 33:
No country shall expel or return (refouler) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories when his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular group or social opinion.
The recognized logic of this is that Canada has solemnly agreed not to refoule anyone inside our borders who claims to be a refugee unless and until Canada has decided that that person's claim is unfounded. The present 1976 Immigration Act reserves to the Minister, on advice of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, or to the Immigration Appeal Board, the power to decide whether a claimant is or is not a real refugee. For several years, senior officials of the Immigration Commission illegally rejected certain claims without letting the Refugee Status Advisory Committee or the Minister see them, until the former Minister stopped them. Since then, they appear to have dragged their heels-by taking many months to arrange typing of the transcript of a claimant's statement under oath for example-until the system became hopelessly backlogged.
Bill C-55 is a renewed drive by the senior officials to exclude most claimants either on the ground that they could have claimed elsewhere or on the ground that they do not have a claim worth listening to. They are to be screened out before coming to the refugee division, which will have the legal authority to decide claims, and deported. This device not only violates Article 33 of the Convention, endangering real refugees, but will also waste time on cases that do go forward to the refugee division. That is the very fault laid against our present refugee determination system.
Let us deal with the safe third country. Is there a real safe third country in the world? The first test is to decide whether the claimant spent any time, other than at an airport in transit, in a country where he or she might have been safe. This is to be decided by looking at a list, made by the Cabinet, of countries that comply with Article 33 of the Convention.
That sounds reasonable at first. However, since Canada refused to hear that person's claim, Canada has no right to assume that the other country will hear it either. Therefore, the other country may do as Canada did, and expel the claimant to somewhere else which could bring the claimant who may be a genuine refugee back to the country of actual persecution. That would violate Canada's Convention obligation not to refoule a refugee even indirectly.
We have seen an example of this only in the last couple of weeks. An individual was sent back to the safe third country, where he was immediately deported. That safe third country was our neighbour to the south. We have been talking about a continental energy policy, but I think we have a continental immigration policy to make sure that certain people do not get into the northern part of North America.
Let me turn to the credibility test. If a claimant passes the safe third country test, he or she is then required to demonstrate a credible basis for the claim. This, defined as having credible and trustworthy evidence upon which the refugee division might find a claim well founded, really means that the refugee division's work is to be done first at the screening, hastily, without a fair chance for the claimant to prepare, and by a panel including an adjudicator who is not competent to decide refugee claims.
If I had to decide for some reason that I must leave Canada because of my political or religious beliefs, I do not believe it would be something I would plan to do for some months, and therefore be able to arrange all the documentation I needed to support my claim to the country to which I was fleeing. Rather I would be probably lucky to flee with the clothes on my back. Most legitimate refugees do not have the opportunity to bring their documentation.
When I was a provincial member, I recall having a case of a citizen from the Ukraine, who was visiting Thunder Bay. She wanted to claim political asylum but there was a catch to the situation. She was divorced, but the divorce papers were in the hands of the Soviet authorities and therefore she could not use
October 16, 1987

the option of marrying a Canadian as a means of staying in Canada.
The point is that it is very easy for non progressive countries that are bound to create refugees of some type to ensure that their citizens do not have the proper documentation available to them. Furthermore, a person is a legitimate refugee likely because his political views differ from those of a fascist or military dictatorship. What assurances are there that such a government would give the Canadian Government accurate information about the refugee?
There must be a process by which each case can be examined on its merit rather than referring to a shopping list of safe third countries to which these refugees can be returned.
Canada has supported some very questionable governments in South America and other parts of the world over the years. We have seen those governments overthrown.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I thank my colleague, the Member for Spadina for his efforts. We will continue to speak to this Bill to give the Government time to reconsider it, and realize that what it is doing is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, does the Hon. Member agree that in some measure part of the abuse of the refugee system lies in the fact that it seems on occasion to be the only way to have access to this country? Perhaps if we could even meet the targets that are set, which we have not done for a number of years, there would be a system in which people would at least think they have a chance to have access to this country.
I agree with the Member when he says that there are many bogus claims of which he does not approve. I do not think any Member of the House approves of that activity. Frustration exists because the system has been bogged down by red tape, which I suppose is necessary in some measure in an immigration system but has been carried too far in our system and has put it into a state of inertia. Would the Member comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) for his comments and his question. I agree that not only in terms of structure but in terms of philosophy we must open up this country. A number of years ago I listened to an individual, whom I will not name but who was a member of the big blue machine out of Queen's Park. He appeared on Canada AM every now and then with two other individuals, representing other political parties, who will also remain nameless. He spoke to a conference in Thunder Bay and argued very forcefully about the need to increase drastically the number of people coming to this country. The traditional family in Canada has 1.2 children, not enough even to sustain the existing population. We must, therefore, open up legal immigration.
Immigration Act, 1976
Ours is a vast country which was populated by immigrants. My father's family came to Canada in the 1790s from the United States, having gone there from the British Isles. Successive generations of my mother's family came directly from Scotland and Ireland to Canada. My family was part of the group that opened up the west. My grandfather homesteaded in Manitoba in a village called Angusville, appropriately enough. I am the son of an immigrant. With the exception of our native Canadians, we are all sons and daughters of immigrants.
The country is changing because the individuals who come here are no longer primarily from Europe. People from the Caribbean, Asia, Africa and all parts of the world come here now. We need those people to work in our factories and to buy the goods which the factories produce.
It is important to develop an immigration policy which allows people to enter the country. As the Hon. Member said, we cannot even meet our quota. We cannot even reunite families to the extent that we would like. Every week constituents of mine come into my office and tell me, for example, that they have been trying for years to get their brother out of country x or their sister or son our of country y. The red tape which they must go through is extremely frustrating.
We need a system which will ensure that those people who want to come to Canada of their own free will to start a new life and look for opportunities are able to do so. In addition, we have a responsibility to accept those legitimate refugees who are forced to leave their homeland for whatever reasons. We need a process which will ensure that the legitimate ones get through and the bogus ones do not. The process must be carried out in a timely and humane manner, in the Canadian way.

Mr. Speaker, as I begin my comments I am reminded of a question asked by Rabbi Gunther Plaut at a meeting in Montreal in the spring. He simply asked why the Government does not tell Canadians the truth. It is a pertinent question which should be asked by all Canadians, and 1 will come back to it during the course of my remarks.
We are debating today a most shameful piece of legislation which illustrates more than any other Bill before this House the duplicity and hypocrisy of the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

speechtext: Order. I ask that the Member not use those types of words when referring to a specific Member of the House.

I will try to heed your admonishment, Mr. Speaker.
Most important, and regrettably, as a result of the actions of the Government, lives will be at risk and human beings will suffer. In the process Canada's international reputation is being torn to shreds.

October 16, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Canadians were deceived by the Government. We were told that there was an emergency. Parliament was called back on August 11, several weeks after 174 Sikhs arrived on the shores of Nova Scotia. The Government held them in detention for several weeks. Extraordinary measures were implemented. Canadians were led to believe that we were subject to various threats to our security. In the final analysis every single person was released by an adjudicator who came to the conclusion that the Government had no grounds whatsoever for holding these persons in detention.
It is laughable to suggest that we are in an emergency situation when we compare our situation to that of other countries. I understand that the Government of Canada was embarrassed recently at a meeting of the executive committee of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees because of its attitude toward refugees. Observers from the refugee-producing countries attend the meetings of this organization.
At this particular meeting there were observers from Pakistan and the Sudan, each of which receive millions of refugees. There were representatives from Somalia, Mexico and Thailand which receive hundreds of thousands of persons seeking asylum or temporary shelter. Not one of those countries are taking restrictive measures. Not one of those countries even mentioned restrictive measures. They simply asked the western countries for help by way of food, medicine, or other goods, in order to cope with the hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of refugees on their borders.
If you can believe it, Mr. Speaker, Canada complained about the 30,000 or so asylum-seekers who have accumulated in our country over the past several years. We almost got booed out of the place. When the International Council of Voluntary Agencies in its statement on the protection of refugees complained about the restrictive measures and the inadequate appeals in the Bill that we are studying here today, quite understandably, the faces of the Canadian delegation turned red.
Is this the international image that we want to keep? Is this in keeping with Canada's humanitarian traditions which we have established over the past 25 or 30 years?
Where was the mellifluous Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) this past August with his words of generosity and compassion? 1 remind the House that only one year and several months ago now, in August of 1986, he said the following. These are the words which he uttered as reported in the press on August 18, 1986. He said, "It is not the presence of 155 frightened human beings searching for freedom and opportunity that is going to undermine Canada or our immigration policies". He was talking about the Tamils who had arrived in the summer of 1986.
What happened in the year? In 1986, the Prime Minister was generous in his attitude toward refugees. A year later, in
1987, he was silent. He had not a word to say. He left the dirty work to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and to the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner), who is sitting here in the House today.
The Prime Minister piped up recently and actually had the audacity to say that refugees are the wave of the future. On September 25 of this year, again as reported in the press, he said that accepting more refugees is going to be the wave of the future. May 1 suggest that the Prime Minister's words ring hollow when compared to the restrictive actions that this Government is taking? But how typical, I would suggest as well. The Government and the Prime Minister promised generosity and compassion, but we get harsh, unconscionable actions. It is no wonder that the people of Canada do not believe a word that he says. It is no wonder that the Government has sunk to such a low standing in the opinion of Canadians.
I come back to the question I asked earlier today at the opening of my remarks. Why not tell the truth? The Government and its spokesmen have misrepresented what honest, well-meaning individuals mean by the concept of universal access. They suggested that we would open the doors to all the refugees in the world, to the 15 million or 20 million of them. They even went so far as to say that we were suggesting that five billion people ought to come to Canada, if one can believe that.
I would like to refer the House to the words of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Friesen) who, in debate in the House on August 13 of this year, as reported at page 8036 of Hansard, stated, "What 1 said was under the Singh decision," that being the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada a year or two ago in 1985, "with respect to the protection under the Charter, there is a possibility of five billion people. Anyone around the world could land on our shores . . . Therefore, potentially every person in the world can come here and claim refugee status. That confirms the numbers I quoted".
The Minister of State for Immigration now has his head buried in his papers. On that same day I was engaged in an exchange with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) who said that he did not believe in the concept of universal access. The Minister, in reference to me, said, "He is saying to Canadians, and they have to understand this, that everyone who decides to come to Canada and claim refugee status should have access". The Minister of State for Immigration piped up and said, "Five billion people". "Five billion people", the Minister of State for Immigration said, as reported at page 8043 of Hansard for August 13, 1987. What kind of nerve does he have to make that type of irresponsible statement? What type of nerve does he have to suggest to Canadians that five billion people may come to our shores?
Are those the actions of a responsible Minister of the Crown? Are those the actions of a responsible Minister of State for Immigration who flouts these kinds of fears and this
October 16, 1987

kind of ridiculous notion before Canadians? Five billion people, he said. It cannot be repeated often enough.
Universal access simply means that we give all people who claim to be refugees and who manage to come to Canada a right to be heard on the merits of their claims. That does not mean that we accept them. Our only obligation-

Mr. Speaker, prior to my comments being interrupted by Royal Assent, I was explaining that the concept of universal access simply means that we give all people who manage to get to our shores and claim to be refugees a full hearing on the merits. Those who are in favour of this concept believe that we must give all persons a chance to prove their case. That does not mean that we have to accept all claimants. Indeed, under the UN Convention the only obligation we have is not to return them to a country where their lives would be in danger. Therefore, we can simply accept people on a temporary basis. If the situation in the country from which they fled corrects itself, we can return them to that country at that time.
It is totally misleading and incorrect to say that we are being flooded by millions of potential claimants. Millions of refugees are not coming to Canada. They have no desire to come here. They wish to return to their own countries. At the meeting of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees executive committee in Geneva, representatives from Somalia, Thailand, and Mexico did not ask Canada or western countries to resettle those refugees. They asked for our aid. Second, we have slammed on visas for most refugee producing countries. Third, we have imposed tremendous fines on transportation companies, so that the vast majority of refugees in the world will be left to struggle in refugee camps, to starve, to be shot at, and to be trampled on. It is misleading to suggest that those refugees in any way pose a threat to the peace of mind and way of life of Canadians, or to suggest that they are arriving in numbers which we cannot handle.
The following questions have been asked by Tory Members. Why should we help those who have managed to come here? Why not choose more from the refugee camps? They have said that they are the deserving ones, as if to say that those who come here on their own are not deserving, are not in need of our protection, or are breaking the rules to come here.
There is a very clear answer to these questions. It is precisely to allow refugees to move spontaneously on their own to a safe haven that the UN Convention exists. It was adopted after World War II when hundreds of thousands of people became victims because they had nowhere to go, no country would accept them. The UN Convention was established to

October 16, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
permit refugees to move spontaneously to seek salvation on their own. It was not to require them to stand in line or to apply at embassies abroad. The Convention was a deviation from the principle that sovereign states had total control over their borders.
Again I remind Hon. Members that it is incorrect, therefore, to suggest that under the UN Convention we are somehow subject to being flooded by hundreds of thousands of claimants from around the world.
Another great promise of the Government was to consult with Canadians. Not a single witness before the legislative committee supported the Bill. I remind the Minister of that fact. I would also suggest that Hon. Members read what the witnesses said.
In particular I should like to quote Professor William Angus from Osgoode Hall, an expert authority on administrative law. He referred to how the Government, in this Bill, was trying to limit access to the courts and to the traditional remedy which people have to apply to the courts for review of a decision made by a government agency or government board. In this case it would be the refugee division.
If we read his testimony before the committee, we see that he referred to the legislation as being unprecedented. He said that he had not seen before a situation where, in order to get the courts to review a decision made by the refugee division, one needed the permission of a judge or needed to apply for leave. Normally one does not have to ask the court for its permission; one has the right to have the court review the decision of an administrative tribunal. It is a long-standing remedy available to citizens which was developed in common law going back hundreds of years.
He went on to say that the provision in Bill C-55 was a most extraordinary provision which might be appropriate for an authoritarian state but completely inappropriate for a democracy such as we have in Canada which has the system of the rule of law. Is that not quite a statement for a professor of law to make before a parliamentary committee?
1 have struggled to find words to express the abhorrence I feel for this wicked, unjust Bill for I do not believe that it belongs on the books. We were told by witnesses that court challenges were already being prepared, that it offends the Charter, that it offends human dignity, that it offends Canadians' sense of fairness, and that it offends human nature which will not submit to arbitrary, heavy-handed measures.
In conclusion, I am reminded of the words of the poet Robert Frost who wrote the following in the poem Mending Wall:
Something there is that doesn't love a wall,
That sends the frozen-ground-swell under it.
And spills the upper boulders in the sun;
And makes gaps even two can pass abreast.
As long as human beings have a breath of life, as long as they have a will to survive, they will find ways around the walls built by bureaucrats. They will find ways to save their lives. They will not linger in refugee camps.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) on his excellent and very thoughtful presentation to the House this afternoon.
For the benefit of all Hon. Members, could he tell us what he thinks in greater detail about the so-called safe third country concept? We know that although certain countries may be a safe haven for individuals coming from certain destinations, they are not necessarily a safe haven for those who come from other countries or countries with different political beliefs.
Further, perhaps the Hon. Member could inform us on what he thinks of the particular provision and what he thinks will be the long-term effect of such a clause, were it to stand up to court challenges. We recognize that there is a distinct possibility that it will not. However, in the unlikely event that it will withstand a court challenge, what does the Hon. Member think will be the long-term effect of such a clause, both in terms of what the direct result would be for individual claimants and in terms of our status as a nation, recognizing that we have been an award winning nation? I am referring to the Nansen Medal which our country merited not long ago. How does he think we will fare in that regard with this new policy?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. The safe third country provision in the Bill sets up a screen. It is a way to screen claimants out of the system. It violates the principle of universal access about which I spoke earlier.
In essence it means that a good many claimants who come to Canada will not have the right to make a claim.
Since Canada happens to be a country which is fairly remote from most refugee producing countries, in essence it means that very few refugees will indeed be eligible to make claims in Canada. Estimates have been made that as many as 80 per cent of claimants will be ruled out as a result of this provision. The only ones who might be eligible, for argument's sake, are people from eastern bloc countries and Warsaw Pact countries who are on holiday to Cuba and deplane when the airplane lands to refuel in Gander. They will be eligible.
However, Afghans who spend some time in Pakistan or other countries prior to coming to Canada will not be eligible. Salvadorans who have spent some time in the United States will not be eligible to make a claim under that provision.
We are putting up a wall around our refugee determination system. For all intents and purposes we are excluding the vast majority of the refugees of the world. Furthermore, the Member will note, if he reads the provision relating to a safe
October 16, 1987

third country, that these countries will be prescribed by Cabinet. In other words, if a person is on a list prescribed by Cabinet, that person is refused, denied, access to the refugee determination system. There is no discretion whatever given to the adjudicator or the member of the refugee division at the hearing to look at the individual situation of the claimant. If the claimant is on a list, he is out of the system, excluded, and not entitled to make a claim. I understand that this is at variance with the practice in many of the European countries which have tried to implement this kind of a system. In France and West Germany there is room for individual determination, even if a person comes from a so-called safe third country.
The Member asked me to speak to the question of effect. I said earlier this summer in this debate and in an article that I wrote that tragic mistakes will be made, undeniably tragic mistakes will be made. I tried not to exaggerate the impact that this would have because we were trying to have a civilized debate. ITowever, what do I mean by saying that tragic mistakes will be made, Mr. Speaker? Very simply, lives will be lost. Human beings will suffer as a result of this particular provision and this legislation. What does it do to Canada's international reputation? As I said earlier, our international reputation is being torn to shreds. Again, I have talked to people who attended the meeting of the executive committee of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in Geneva recently where Canadian officials were all but booed out of the room.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was at the meeting and there was no booing. Canada was applauded for its stand. The Member might like to get his facts straight. As for the situation in Europe today, in most cases people from other European countries are turned away at the border with no appeals. They have none of the kinds of protections we see in Bill C-55.
When the Member speaks and writes articles about a safe third country, perhaps he should read the legislation and discover its accuracy. If the Member looks at the amended Bill, as part of the eligibility requirements in an inland hearing there is absolutely no notion of a safe third country being a consideration. The notion of a safe third country will occur at a border point when, in the judgment of the immigration official, there is no need for protection in Canada. That judgment is then appealed to an inquiry with an adjudicator and a refugee board member. It can further be appealed to the Federal Court of Canada, and it is always appealable to the Minister. There are three levels of appeal in the Canadian system in those few cases which will occur at border points.
You are kidding yourself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

There are three levels of appeal from an administrative judgment, Mr. Speaker. The European system has no appeal in most cases from similar administrative judgments. People are sitting across the way shaking their heads. They are dead wrong.
